Alice.summary: In fiction, there are propositions that are implicitly true in addition to explicit truth, such as common-sense facts.

Bob.summary: There is no such thing as implicit truth in fiction in addition to explicit truth, because sequels can create unreasonable contradictions.

c1.text: In 'A Study in Scarlet', the statement 'Holmes is a detective' appears explicitly, so <Holmes is a detective> is explicitly true in this novel.

c2.text: Nowhere in 'A Study in Scarlet' is there any explicit statement about the number of Holmes's nostrils.

c3.text: It is common knowledge that Holmes is human within the work, and humans generally have two nostrils.

c4.text: The proposition <Holmes has two nostrils> is implicitly true in 'A Study in Scarlet'.

c5.text: In fiction, there are propositions that are implicitly true in addition to explicit truth.

c6.text: Propositions such as <The earth is round> and <All humans die> are implicitly true in 'A Study in Scarlet'.

c7.text: Sequels to fictional works have the power to determine the truth of things not made explicit in the original work.

c8.text: If a sequel 'A Study in Red' explicitly states Holmes had three nostrils since birth, <Holmes has three nostrils> is true in 'A Study in Scarlet'.

c9.text: If <Holmes has two nostrils> is implicitly true in 'A Study in Scarlet', Holmes must have both two and three nostrils at the same time in 'A Study in Scarlet'.

c10.text: Holmes having both two and three nostrils at the same time in 'A Study in Scarlet' is an unreasonable consequence.

c11.text: There is no such thing as implicit truth in fiction in addition to explicit truth.

c12.text: Any proposition must be either true or false in a particular fiction.

c13.text: The proposition <Holmes has two nostrils> could be true in 'A Study in Scarlet' and later become false.

c14.text: The proposition <The earth is round> is true in 'A Study in Scarlet'.

a.note: Alice accepts common-sense implicit truths, but does not presuppose the principle of bivalence for every proposition in fiction.

b.note: Bob argues that <Holmes has two nostrils> was never implicitly true to begin with, not that its truth value changes over time.

h1.text: A sequel to 'A Study in Scarlet' contains an explicit statement that the earth is round.

c.note: According to Bob, if a sequel explicitly states 'The earth is round', that proposition becomes true in the original work.
